questions.q: Why must num_heads divide d_model evenly?
options: It doesn't actually need to; any combination works
Because each attention head operates on its own slice of size d_model / num_heads (the head dimension), which must be a whole number
Because PyTorch requires num_heads to be a power of two
Because num_heads controls the number of transformer layers, not attention width
questions.explain: Multi-head attention splits the d_model-sized vector into num_heads equal slices, each of size d_model / num_heads, so that division must come out even.

questions.q: Why is increasing d_model generally more expensive in parameter count than increasing num_layers by the same factor?
options: They cost exactly the same either way

Because the dominant per-layer projections (attention and feed-forward) are quadratic in d_model, so total parameters scale roughly with num_layers * d_model^2 — doubling d_model roughly quadruples each layer's parameters, while doubling num_layers only doubles the total
Because num_layers has no effect on parameter count at all
Because d_model only affects the final output layer, not the transformer blocks
questions.explain: Attention and feed-forward projections inside each block scale quadratically with d_model, so widening the model is more expensive per unit increase than deepening it, which scales linearly.

questions.q: Why does increasing max_seq_len (context length) carry a different kind of cost than increasing d_model or num_layers?
options: It carries no additional cost at all
Attention's compute and memory cost grows quadratically, O(T^2), with sequence length, since every position attends to every other position — unlike parameter count, which doesn't depend on seq_len
It only affects the model's final linear head, not attention
It decreases compute cost because longer sequences are processed in fewer batches
questions.explain: Because every position attends to every other position, the compute/memory cost of a single forward pass grows quadratically with sequence length, a cost separate from parameter count scaling with num_layers * d_model^2.

questions.q: A tiny GPT is scaled up, and training loss keeps dropping while validation loss stalls or starts rising. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The learning rate is too low
The model has outgrown the dataset (overfitting) and needs more data, more regularization, or a smaller model — not just more training steps
The model architecture is broken and must be rebuilt from scratch
This is expected and requires no action
questions.explain: A widening gap between falling training loss and stalled/rising validation loss is the classic overfitting signature; the fix is more data, stronger regularization, or a smaller model relative to the dataset, not more steps on the same data.

questions.q: What is the core practical takeaway from 'scaling laws' research, as applied to scaling a tiny GPT?
options: Only model width matters; depth and data size are irrelevant
Model size should always be maximized regardless of dataset size
Scaling just one lever in isolation gives diminishing or negative returns; capacity increases are reliably useful only when paired with proportionally more data and compute
Scaling laws prove that perplexity cannot be used to evaluate larger models
questions.explain: The scaling-laws insight is that loss improves smoothly and predictably when model size, data, and compute are scaled together — turning up only one of those levers tends to yield poor or even negative returns.
